title: Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21)
hook: a king and queen seize a man's family land by lies

segments.voice: Yesterday, under the broom tree: bread, water, sleep, and a second touch. Your line was the journey is too great for you.
screen: `THE JOURNEY IS TOO GREAT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: "The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee." That's a man named Naboth, saying no to a king. His vineyard sits right next to King Ahab's palace in Jezreel, and Ahab wants it for a vegetable garden. He even makes a fair offer: a better vineyard, or the full price in money. Naboth refuses. And the king of Israel goes home, lies down on his bed, turns his face away, and won't eat. Over a garden.

To Naboth it isn't real estate. It's inheritance, the land his family has held, and the law of Moses treats land that way. In Leviticus, God says: "The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine." Some things are not for sale, even to a king. Now Queen Jezebel finds her husband sulking, and says, "Dost thou now govern the kingdom of Israel?" I'll get you the vineyard. What she does is chilling because it all looks legal. She writes letters in Ahab's name and seals them with his seal. She has the elders of the city proclaim a fast, set Naboth on high among the people, and set two men across from him to accuse him. They say he blasphemed God and the king. The crowd takes him outside the city and stones him to death. Letters, seals, a public fast, witnesses: every piece of a proper trial, used for theft and murder. Then Ahab goes down to take possession of his garden, and there Elijah meets him, with a question that strips the paperwork away: "Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?" Ahab's reply is almost a confession: "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" And Elijah says, "I have found thee." The chapter doesn't end in simple triumph. When Ahab hears the judgment, he tears his clothes, fasts, and goes about quietly, and the text says God takes notice that he has humbled himself. But the vineyard stays a name for something people still see: the powerful taking a home through lies dressed as law.
screen: `THE LAND SHALL NOT BE SOLD FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Picture someone losing their place: a neighbor facing eviction, a family pushed out by rising rent, people driven from their land by war, an aging parent leaving the house they raised you in. Stay with them at their front door without looking away, then ask what one real thing you could do. If you pray, you can hold them before God.
Naboth's vineyard. A man won't sell his family's land, and a king and queen take it with forged letters and false witnesses, until a prophet names it.
Your line: not for sale. A small vineyard, and a prophet who would not look away. That's day seven hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Some Christians point to Naboth's vineyard when they speak up about land seizure, eviction and abuse of power, and churches sometimes read it alongside the prophets' warnings about those who add field to field.

notes: 'Turns his face to the wall' paraphrases 21:4 ('turned away his face'); confirm.
The legal-looking machinery (letters, seal, fast, Naboth set on high, two witnesses, stoning outside the city) follows 21:8–13; 'sons of Belial' is left out.
The judgment oracle (21:19b–24, dogs licking blood) is not retold; Ahab's repentance (21:27–29) is summarized. Confirm the balance.
'The law of Moses treats land that way' leans on Leviticus 25:23 and Numbers 36:7; confirm.
howItsDone's reference to 'those who add field to field' is Isaiah 5:8 (paraphrased, not quoted).
